medium: gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper

highlight.text: This sensitively painted portrait was made for the collection of the Mughal emperor Akbar who was curious about the tenets of Jainism.

source.author: The Cleveland Museum of Art

Welch: Mughal miniatures were made in “the technique of opaque watercolor or gouache painting”

work.text: Alluding to his wisdom, this white-clad Jain monk carries a manuscript under his left arm, bound with a red cover. Otherwise he carries a Jain monk’s basic accouterments: whisk broom, staff, and pot.

source.author: The Cleveland Museum of Art
source.title: Jain Ascetic Walking Along a Riverbank

work.text: Basawan’s achievement was crucial to the development of [Jahangiri] portraiture in the early seventeenth century, an astonishing attainment since he was also [instrumental] in the formation of the quite different early Mughal style.

source.author: Milo Cleveland Beach
source.title: The Imperial Image: Paintings for the Mughal Court
source.publisher: Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: He admired the explanations of the Jain monks who regularly attended the emperor’s weekly discussion sessions among members of different religious groups.

source.author: The Cleveland Museum of Art
source.title: Jain Ascetic Walking Along a Riverbank

moment.text: Zoroastrians, Jains, Hindus and Muslims of all sects, and Christians joined in these serious all-night conversations, during which the emperor’s questions often must have been as upsetting as they were penetrating.

matters.text: Basawan, with minimal means, suggests that his subjects are part of our world.
